column1: # MODE: PROD
# What this skill needs on the target machine at runtime, and how badly.
# installer/build.sh generates install.sh's dependency tables from every skill's
# copy of this file; the shared installer/tools.tsv says how to verify a tool and
# how to install it, so the install instructions are written once, not per skill.
# Columns, tab-separated:
#   tool       tool id; must have a row in installer/tools.tsv
#   condition  <uname -s glob>:<uname -m glob> the row applies to, e.g. *:* or
#              Darwin:arm64 — a bash case pattern, so | may join alternatives
#   strength   hard = the skill does not work without the tool, so the installer
#              refuses to install this skill and exits non-zero
#              soft = the skill degrades honestly, so the installer installs it
#              and warns which capability is lost
#   why        one line naming the capability that is lost without the tool
# Line-oriented TSV rather than JSON on purpose: rjq is itself declared here, so a
# format that needed rjq to read it could not be read on the machine that is
# missing it. awk and sed parse this.
# No rows: the skill ships two prebuilt rust binaries (interactive-shell, the
# PTY wrapper; interactive-shell-input, the socket client) and needs nothing
# else on the target. Neither is committed or built at install time — the
# release/CI builds them against binaries.tsv and install.sh copies them. They
# depend only on libc and serde, allocate the PTY through libc directly, and
# speak JSONL on stdout and a 0600 unix socket, so there is no external tool to
# verify: no jq (the agent parses the JSONL), no rjq, no terminal library.
# The child program the wrapper drives (nano, mc, lynx, a pager) is the user's
# choice at call time, not a dependency of the skill — the wrapper is generic
# and never assumes a particular TUI is installed.
tool
